problems.title: The stated softmax \(\ell_1\)-Lipschitz constant misses an essential contribution
problems.source_location: Lemma 2, Eq. (12), PDF p. 8; Lemma 4, Eqs. (109)–(110), PDF p. 45.
claim: Paraphrase: Lemma 2, PDF p. 8, Eq. (12), and its expanded Lemma 4, PDF p. 45, Eqs. (109)–(110), state that whenever both vectors have spread at most \(\delta>0\),
analysis: Take \(z=(0,0,0)\), \(\bar z=(0.01,0,0)\), and \(\delta=0.01\). Both spreads satisfy the hypothesis. The exact change is \(\|s(z)-s(\bar z)\|_1=4(e^{0.01}-1)/(3(e^{0.01}+2))\approx0.004451827\), but the claimed bound is \((e^{0.01}/3)0.01\approx0.003366834\). The first probability bound remains valid; the Lipschitz inequality does not.

The Jacobian is \(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\): column \(j\) contributes \(p_j(1-p_j)\) on the diagonal and the same total off diagonal, so its induced \(\ell_1\) norm is \(\max_j2p_j(1-p_j)\). At uniform probabilities this exceeds \(1/L\) whenever \(L>2\). The earlier cited softmax result contains an analogous problematic constant; no priority claim is made.
result: The stated softmax Lipschitz constant is false, so later stability bounds cannot use that constant without a new derivation. No experimental performance reversal follows from this calculation.
repair: Use the exact induced Jacobian norm \(\max_j2p_j(1-p_j)\). On a fixed support of size \(n\), \(\min\{1/2,2e^\delta/n\}\) is a safe bound; keep probability and derivative constants distinct and rederive downstream estimates.
problems.impact_rationale: The explicit within-domain counterexample falsifies the softmax Lipschitz constant on which the central attention-stability derivation relies; Major is warranted.
problems.existing_correction_status: The stated local proposal is retained; the current paper or author source still has the identified behavior. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: The heavy-hitter support-change proof drops common-support normalization terms
problems.source_location: Lemma 6, PDF pp. 54–56, especially Eqs. (229)–(230), PDF p. 55.
claim: Lemma 6, PDF pp. 54–56, seeks a Lipschitz comparison of \(s_b(z)\) and \(s_{\bar b}(\bar z)\), with \(b=m(z)\), \(\bar b=m(\bar z)\), \(k\) selected logits, selected spread at most \(\delta\), and gap at least \(\Delta>0\). In Eq. (229), it applies a fixed-mask bound at an intermediate vector. In Eq. (230), PDF p. 55, it bounds the full distance between two differently masked softmaxes by contributions on indices where the masks differ. Both steps need conditions or terms that are absent.
analysis: The endpoint pair \(z=(1,2,0)\) and \(\bar z=(1,0,2)\) has the respective top-two masks in the claim, selected spread \(\delta=1\) and positive gap \(\Delta=1\), so it meets the stated endpoint conditions without a tie.

At \(\bar z=(1,0,2)\), compare masks \((1,1,0)\) and \((1,0,1)\). Their common first coordinate changes because the two normalizers differ. The full \(\ell_1\) distance is \(2e/(e+1)\approx1.462117\), whereas summing only the two changed-support coordinates gives \(1\). Thus Eq. (230) drops a positive contribution even without a support-boundary tie; the separate fixed-mask intermediate step also needs its own domain conditions.

The intermediate fixed-mask step is also unjustified: \(z=(0,0,-10)\) and \(\bar z=(0,-10,0)\) each have own-support spread \(0\) and gap \(10\), but applying the old mask to \(\bar z\) selects logits of spread \(10\). The endpoint assumption \(\delta=0.01\) therefore does not hold at that intermediate vector.
result: The displayed support-change estimate is not a valid proof of the claimed bound. A corrected argument must retain common-support normalization changes.
repair: On the stated positive-gap domain, the weaker valid constant is \(\max\{C_{k,\delta},1/\Delta\}\), where \(C_{k,\delta}\) is a valid fixed-support constant. Different supports require an input change of at least \(2\Delta\), while probability-vector distance is at most \(2\). This avoids the invalid intermediate steps but does not restore the claimed favorable dependence on \(k\).
problems.impact_rationale: The proof drops a nonzero common-support normalization contribution in a central masked-attention stability argument. This substantial derivation error warrants Major even without an empirical ranking reversal.
problems.existing_correction_status: The stated local proposal is retained; the current paper or author source still has the identified behavior. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: The multilayer loss bound can be negative because the geometric-series formula lacks its domain condition
problems.source_location: Theorem 2, Eq. (11), PDF p. 8; Corollary 1, Appendix F.3, Eq. (79), PDF p. 42.
claim: Theorem 2, PDF p. 8, Eq. (11), and Corollary 1 in Appendix F.3, PDF p. 42, Eq. (79), give
analysis: The hypotheses do not require \(q>1\). On the intended bounded domain, choose dimension and sequence length \(d=L=2\), depth \(\tau=1\), bounds \(B=\Xi=1\), and LayerNorm scale \((0.6,0.6)\), shift zero, and \(\epsilon=1\). Valid conservative attention constants \((\lambda_X,\lambda_W,\lambda_V)=(0.01,0.02,2)\) give the paper's block constants \(q=0.7272\) and \(\lambda_\theta=3.8544\). With \(\alpha=1\), its loss constant is \(1+0.7272[1+3.8544/(2(0.7272-1))]\approx-3.410116\).

For an actual positive difference, take zero attention/feed-forward weights and input tokens \((0.5,-0.5)\). Two LayerNorm applications give \[(0.1554963166,-0.1554963166)\]. Comparing readouts \((1,0)\) and \((0,0)\) with sample loss \(|f|\) yields loss difference \(0.1554963166>0\), despite the negative claimed upper bound. All outputs and readout norms stay within the stated unit bounds.
result: The unrestricted geometric-series simplification is false on an admissible bounded domain. It is undefined at q equal to one and can be negative below one; this does not imply the experiments used that regime.
repair: Retain the nonnegative finite sum \(\alpha[\Xi+q^\tau+(\lambda_\theta/L)\sum_{j=0}^{\tau-1}q^j]\). The sum is \((q^\tau-1)/(q-1)\) for \(q\ne1\) and \(\tau\) at \(q=1\). Alternatively impose \(q>1\) for the looser printed bound. This repairs only the composition step; its attention constants still require justification.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: An admissible bounded-domain transformer gives a negative purported loss Lipschitz bound while its actual loss difference is positive. This directly falsifies the main composition theorem as stated and warrants Major.
problems.existing_correction_status: The stated local proposal is retained; the current paper or author source still has the identified behavior. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: Released attention applies dropout during evaluation
problems.source_location: Appendix D, PDF p. 29; released multihead_attention.py, scaled_dot_prod.
claim: Appendix D, PDF p. 29, specifies dropout probability \(0.01\). In released multihead_attention.py, scaled_dot_prod calls functional dropout with the supplied dropout_p and the default active training mode. MultiHeadAttention.forward supplies the same positive probability in evaluation mode.
analysis: A functional dropout call using its default training flag continues to mask activations after the enclosing module enters eval mode unless the module's training flag is passed. This is a contract mismatch for the released attention path; published-run provenance and numerical effects are not inferred.
result: Current attention remains stochastic in evaluation mode; no remeasurement establishes the size of its effect on model rankings or loss surfaces.
repair: Pass the enclosing module’s training state to functional dropout, or supply zero dropout probability during evaluation.

problems.title: ListOps skips one example and divides evaluation totals by the full dataset size
problems.source_location: Appendix D (ListOps implementation); released ListOps training and evaluation denominator calculations.
claim: In the released listops.py, batch_yielder and evaluate stop at the dataset size minus one, omit the final item, and divide evaluation totals by the full dataset size.
analysis: With \(N=5\) uniformly correct examples, the loop counts only \(4\) but divides by \(5\), reporting \(80\%\) instead of \(100\%\). The loss denominator has the same mismatch. The relative effect on a full benchmark depends on its size; no substantial benchmark impact is established.
result: The released evaluator omits one example; at the stated holdout size \(N=2000\), this isolated accounting error is at most \(0.05\) percentage points and does not explain the reported convergence gains.
repair: Use the full dataset size as the exclusive loop and slice boundary, then divide the totals by the number of examples actually processed.
problems.impact_rationale: The released evaluator omits one example; at the stated holdout size \(N=2000\), this isolated accounting error is at most \(0.05\) percentage points and does not explain the reported convergence gains.

problems.title: The loss-landscape code does not compute the direction-normalized estimator in Eq. (306)
problems.source_location: Figure 5, PDF p. 10; Appendix G.5, PDF pp. 62–65, especially Eq. (306), PDF p. 63.
claim: Figure 5, PDF p. 10, Appendix G.5, PDF pp. 62–65, and Eq. (306), PDF p. 63, interpret neighboring loss-grid differences as directional estimates of the loss Lipschitz constant. The displayed estimator divides by both the coordinate step \(\epsilon\) and the norm of the perturbation direction:
analysis: Let \(\theta=2\), \(L(\theta)=\theta\), direction \(v=2\), and step \(\epsilon=0.005\). The loss change is \(0.01\). Dividing only by \(\epsilon\) gives \(2\), whereas the direction-normalized quotient in Eq. (306) is \(1\). The released quotient changes under direction rescaling, so it is a different estimator.
result: Omitting direction norms changes the measured landscape statistic; the required norms are unavailable for reconstructing corrected published curves, and no performance reversal follows.
repair: For horizontal edges, divide each difference by \(h_x\|\vartheta_1\|\); for vertical edges, divide by \(h_y\|\vartheta_2\|\). Normalize these two sets before pooling their quantiles, because the direction norms can differ. The norms must use the same parameter metric as the theorem being evaluated; with the paper’s tuple norm, this is the maximum spectral norm across matrix parameter blocks, with an explicit convention for vectors and auxiliary learned parameters. Alternatively normalize both complete directions to unit norm in that metric before producing the grid.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

These substantial theoretical failures support Major independently of the unmeasured empirical effects.
